displayQuote: Just give them two and two and let them add it up

meta.title: Who really said "Just give them two and two and let them add it up"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Billy Wilder said it in an AFI seminar, printed in Conversations with the Great Moviemakers (Knopf, 2006), p. 320 — but he credited Ernst Lubitsch, unverified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Just give them two and two and let them add it up'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilder really said it, at an AFI seminar published in 2006. He credited Lubitsch — and Quote Investigator has found no citation of Lubitsch saying it. The documented trail.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Wilder said it aloud in a seminar at the American Film Institute; the transcript was published as the Billy Wilder chapter of Conversations with the Great Moviemakers of Hollywood’s Golden Age at the American Film Institute, edited by George Stevens Jr. (Alfred A. Knopf, 2006), quote page 320, where Quote Investigator verified it on paper ↗. One honest complication: Wilder was voicing advice he said he had learned from Ernst Lubitsch, and Quote Investigator has found no citation in which Lubitsch spoke these words — so the sentence is documented as Wilder’s spoken line, credited by Wilder to someone else.

source.heading: The AFI seminar transcript

docMeta.dd: Conversations with the Great Moviemakers of Hollywood’s Golden Age at the American Film Institute

At an American Film Institute seminar. The Wilder chapter is dated 13 December 1978 and its footnote records segments from seminars of 7 January 1976 and 3 March 1986; Quote Investigator concludes only that the line was said on or before 3 March 1986.
Edited by George Stevens Jr., Alfred A. Knopf, New York, 2006. Quote page 320.
“A tip from Lubitsch: Let the audience add up two plus two. They’ll love you forever.” — Cameron Crowe, Conversations with Wilder (Knopf, 1999), p. 357.

source.excerpt: This is what I learned from Ernst Lubitsch. He had a real touch, a gift of involving the audience into writing the script with him as it was unfolding on the screen. … He said, “No, just give them two and two and let them add it up. They’re going to do it for you. And they’re going to have fun with it. They’re going to play the game with you.”
trail: On or before 3 March 1986 — the earliest instance located. Wilder’s AFI seminar remarks, published as a chapter in Conversations with the Great Moviemakers of Hollywood’s Golden Age at the American Film Institute (Knopf, 2006), p. 320. Quote Investigator verified this on paper and found nothing earlier ↗.

October 1986 — a plainer public version. A Mitsubishi television advertisement carrying Wilder’s remarks ran in American Film: let people reach for it, let them add it up, don’t spell it out. Quote Investigator verified the advertisement on paper ↗.
1999 — the wording that went everywhere. “Wilder’s Tips for Writers,” item seven, in Cameron Crowe’s Conversations with Wilder (Knopf, 1999) ↗, p. 357 — and it credits Lubitsch by name.
2011–2012 — inherited by the next generation. Vince Gilligan reaches for “the old Billy Wilder quote” in The New York Times ↗; Andrew Stanton calls it “the unifying theory of two plus two” at TED ↗.
source.cutTag: AFI seminar, on or before 3 March 1986
source.excerptNote: Note the quotation marks inside the quotation: Wilder is voicing Lubitsch, not speaking in his own person. That is why the credit is genuinely split — the words are documented as coming out of Wilder’s mouth, and documented nowhere as coming out of Lubitsch’s.

author.name: Billy Wilder
author.heading: Billy Wilder
author.bio: Born 22 June 1906 in Sucha, in the Galicia region of Austria-Hungary, Wilder fled Europe and became a naturalised American citizen in 1939 — the same year he co-wrote Ninotchka for Ernst Lubitsch, the director he spent the rest of his life calling his teacher. Over the next three decades he made Double Indemnity, Sunset Boulevard, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, and became Hollywood’s most quotable craftsman: a writer-director whose advice about writing was as sharp as his dialogue. He died on 27 March 2002.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual: the man everyone credits really did say it. The tangles are one layer up (the mentor Wilder handed the credit to) and one layer down (the wording that actually circulates).

items.why: Wilder introduced the line as Lubitsch’s, not his own — “this is what I learned from Ernst Lubitsch” — and Crowe’s 1999 tip list repeats the credit outright. But Quote Investigator has found no citation in which Lubitsch said these words ↗, and suggests the advice may have reached Wilder in private conversation. Treat Lubitsch as the man Wilder thanked, not a documented speaker.

items.who: Billy Wilder — but not in these words
items.why: The internet’s favourite form is “Let the audience add up two plus two. They’ll love you forever,” which is genuinely Wilder’s — but it comes from the tip list in Cameron Crowe’s 1999 book, not from the seminar. The versions ending “…and let them come up with four” are later restatements by other filmmakers; Vince Gilligan flagged his own as a misquote in The New York Times ↗.

The teaching handbook Outspoken!: How to Improve Writing and Speaking Skills Through Poetry Performance (Heinemann, 2006) offers “put two and two on the page for your reader, but let them add it up” as a paraphrase of Bradbury, per Quote Investigator’s survey ↗. It is presented as a paraphrase, and no Bradbury source is given.

items.who: An unnamed “director in a trade-paper statement”
items.why: Profiled in Contemporary Authors: Autobiography Series, the novelist Daniel Fuchs passed on “let people reach for it, let them add it up” without naming anyone. Quote Investigator conjectures Fuchs had read Wilder’s 1986 Mitsubishi advertisement in a trade paper — an early example of the advice shedding its author.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilder said it, out loud, teaching at the American Film Institute; the transcript is printed and page-cited. What remains open is the man Wilder said he got it from — Quote Investigator credits Wilder with popularising the arithmetic metaphor, has found no citation in which Lubitsch spoke these words, and has located no earlier source ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wilder’s whole point was contempt for contempt. The bad director, in his telling, stops the film to explain it: now listen to me, you idiots, put down the popcorn bag, two and two is four. The good one trusts the audience to do the arithmetic in the dark, and the audience — flattered, busy, complicit — ends up writing the scene alongside him. That trust is the engine of the “Lubitsch touch” Wilder spent his career trying to inherit, and it is why the line has outlived the seminar it was said in.

The advice travelled further than almost anything Wilder wrote for the screen, and it travelled by mutation. In a 1986 magazine advertisement he gave a plainer version; in Cameron Crowe’s 1999 book it became a numbered tip; by the time Vince Gilligan reached for it in 2011 to explain the last shot of a Breaking Bad episode, he prefaced it by admitting he was about to misquote it. He was right, and it did not matter — the idea survives every rewording, which is arguably the best evidence that it is true.
context.detailsSummary: How the line spread, in documented steps
detailsBody: On or before 3 March 1986 — AFI seminar. The earliest instance Quote Investigator located: Wilder, teaching at the American Film Institute, describes what he learned from Lubitsch and voices the two-and-two line. Published in 2006.

October 1986 — a magazine advertisement. Wilder appears in a Mitsubishi campaign in American Film with a plainer form of the same thought: let people reach for it, let them add it up, don’t spell it out.

1987 — the advice goes anonymous. The author Daniel Fuchs, profiled in Contemporary Authors: Autobiography Series, quotes the same counsel from an unnamed “director in a trade-paper statement.” Quote Investigator conjectures Fuchs had seen the Wilder advertisement.

1999 — the famous wording. Cameron Crowe’s Conversations with Wilder prints eleven “Wilder’s Tips for Writers.” Number seven is the version the internet now quotes, and it hands the credit back to Lubitsch.

2006–2012 — adopted by the next generation. Screenwriters Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio cite Wilder on a DVD commentary; Vince Gilligan invokes “the old Billy Wilder quote” in The New York Times; and Andrew Stanton, at TED, calls it “the unifying theory of two plus two” without naming Wilder at all.
context.pull: Lubitsch was not the kind of director who hammered it down — and Wilder spent a career learning to let you do the adding.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article "Storytelling: Just Give Them Two and Two and Let Them Add It Up" concludes Billy Wilder popularised the saying at the American Film Institute on or before 3 March 1986; quotes him verbatim from Conversations with the Great Moviemakers of Hollywood's Golden Age at the American Film Institute (ed. George Stevens Jr., Knopf, 2006), quote page 320, marked "Verified on paper"; states that QI has not found a citation in which Ernst Lubitsch spoke these words; and documents the October 1986 Mitsubishi advertisement in American Film, the 1987 Daniel Fuchs profile in Contemporary Authors, the 1999 Crowe tip list at page 357, the 2006 Outspoken! Ray Bradbury paraphrase, the 2006 Video Business Pirates commentary note, the 2011 Gilligan interview and the 2012 Stanton TED talk.

Billy Wilder was born 22 June 1906 in Sucha, Galicia, Austria-Hungary, died 27 March 2002, was naturalised as a US citizen in 1939, worked as a film director, screenwriter and producer, and collaborated with fellow emigre Ernst Lubitsch on Ninotchka (1939).
Wikiquote's Billy Wilder page gives his dates as 22 June 1906 – 27 March 2002 and does NOT contain any "two and two" / "two plus two" / "let the audience add it up" quotation in any section.
Conversations with Wilder by Cameron Crowe was published by Knopf (distributed by Random House) in 1999, 373 pages, ISBN 0375406603 — consistent with the quote being at page 357.

Internet Archive holds Conversations with the great moviemakers of Hollywood's golden age at the American Film Institute, dated 2006, published New York: Vintage Books, ISBN 9781400033140, 710 pages, with a table of contents that includes a Billy Wilder chapter. (Confirmed via https://archive.org/metadata/conversationswit0000unse_j6f1 — this is the Vintage paperback, not the Knopf hardcover QI paginates.)

Andrew Stanton's TED2012 talk transcript contains verbatim: "And we would call this the unifying theory of two plus two. Make the audience put things together. Don't give them four, give them two plus two." — with no mention of Wilder or Lubitsch in that passage.

The New York Times ArtsBeat interview of 9 October 2011 contains Vince Gilligan saying verbatim: "But there's the old Billy Wilder quote, which I am going to misquote, that if you give the audience 2 plus 2 and let them add it up to 4 themselves, they'll love you forever."
